lead: Centrifugal and reciprocating pumps move water by adding energy to it. This unit shows how each pump works, how head and efficiency are found, where cavitation sets in, and how performance curves guide selection. After it you can read a pump test, check NPSH, and compute slip and air-vessel savings.
about: The unit starts with 7.1, a short family tree of pumps. 7.2 opens the centrifugal pump and follows water from suction pipe to volute casing. 7.3 turns that path into head, efficiency and impeller work equations. 7.4 uses those equations for minimum starting speed and for pumps in series or parallel. 7.5 explains NPSH and cavitation, the limit on suction lift. 7.6 reads performance curves and adds pump specific speed. 7.7 switches to the reciprocating pump, its indicator diagram and slip. 7.8 adds air vessels and calculates work saved. The chapters share one thread: energy added by the pump, losses inside it, and the safe operating point.

chapters.idea: Pumps are grouped by how they add energy: rotodynamic pumps use a spinning impeller, positive-displacement pumps trap and push fixed volumes.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this classification in detail, so keep it short: a family tree with rotodynamic (centrifugal, axial, mixed flow) and positive displacement (reciprocating, rotary). Define pump, rotodynamic, positive displacement, suction and delivery. Give one line each on deep-well (borewell) pumps as multistage centrifugal, jet pumps, and gear or vane pumps. Use Indian examples: a UPI office water tank, a Chennai borewell. Do not derive performance.

figure.aria: A family tree splits pumps into rotodynamic and positive-displacement branches, with centrifugal and reciprocating examples.

chapters.example: A pump has a rotating impeller with curved vanes and delivers 20 L/s at 1450 rpm. Classify it in the pump family tree. Name one positive-displacement pump used for a small high-pressure hand pump.
chapters.trap: Do not call a centrifugal pump a positive-displacement pump; it is rotodynamic and its flow changes with head.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 pressure and head; no pump theory needed.
chapters.leave: Detailed performance, NPSH and slip to 7.2-7.8; pipe friction to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A centrifugal pump spins water outward in an impeller, and a volute casing slows that water so velocity becomes pressure.
chapters.depth: Cover components: suction pipe with foot valve and strainer, impeller (open, semi-open, closed), eye, vanes, volute casing, diffuser ring, delivery pipe, shaft and gland. Explain working step by step: priming, low pressure at the eye, atmospheric pressure pushes water in, rotation gives kinetic energy, volute or diffuser converts velocity to pressure. Some syllabi call it rotodynamic pump; mention volute and whirlpool chambers, and one line on deep-well or borewell multistage pumps. No velocity triangles.

figure.aria: Water moves from the suction pipe to the impeller eye, gains energy in the vanes, and leaves through the volute casing to the delivery pipe.

chapters.example: A centrifugal pump lifts water from a sump 3 m below the pump centreline and delivers it to a tank 12 m above the pump. The suction pipe has a foot valve and strainer. Draw the flow path from sump to tank and state where priming is needed and why.
chapters.trap: Priming is not optional; a dry casing cannot create suction because air density is too low.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 Bernoulli equation and pressure measurement; Unit 1 pressure.
chapters.leave: Head equations, velocity triangles, NPSH and curves to 7.3-7.6; pipe losses to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Impeller work raises head; only part becomes manometric head, the rest is lost to hydraulic, mechanical and volumetric inefficiencies.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach the full derivation, so keep it compact but exam-ready: velocity triangles at inlet and outlet, Euler head H_e = (u₂V_w2 − u₁V_w1)/g for a pump, work done per second per unit weight; manometric head H_m = pressure head across pump + velocity head at delivery; suction head H_s, delivery head H_d, friction heads h_fs and h_fd; manometric efficiency η_man = gH_m/(u₂V_w2), mechanical efficiency, volumetric efficiency, overall efficiency. Define H, Q, N, u, V_w, V_f. Show that H_m < Euler head. Some syllabi call it work done by impeller. No full pump test.

figure.aria: Shaft work becomes Euler head in the impeller; hydraulic losses reduce it to manometric head, and overall efficiency compares output with input.

chapters.example: A centrifugal pump runs at 1450 rpm. The impeller outlet diameter is 300 mm and the outlet vane angle is 30° measured from the tangent. The radial velocity at outlet is 3 m/s. The manometric head is 22 m. Find the Euler head and the manometric efficiency. Take the inlet whirl as zero.
chapters.trap: Use absolute velocity components in Euler head, not the blade speed alone; and put H_m on the manometric side, not Euler head.
chapters.prereq: 7.2 components; Unit 6 velocity triangles and Euler turbomachine equation; Unit 3 Bernoulli.
chapters.leave: Minimum speed, series and parallel, NPSH and curves to 7.4-7.6; pipe friction to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A centrifugal pump cannot lift until its impeller head exceeds the manometric head, and pumps can be combined in series for head or in parallel for flow.
chapters.depth: Derive minimum starting speed by equating Euler head at shut-off to manometric head: N_min = (60/πD)√(gH_m/η_man) for the ideal case, with η_man = 1 if efficiency is not used. Define D, H_m, η_man. Series: same Q, heads add, total H = H1 + H2. Parallel: same H, flows add, total Q = Q1 + Q2. For identical pumps, series doubles head at the same Q and parallel doubles flow at the same H. Use pump curves only qualitatively; full curves in 7.6.

figure.aria: Three lines show one pump, two pumps in series with double head at the same flow, and two pumps in parallel with double flow at the same head.

chapters.example: A centrifugal pump has the characteristic H = 40 − 0.25Q, with H in m and Q in L/s. Two identical pumps are connected in series and in parallel. Find the head at Q = 40 L/s for one pump, two pumps in series, and two pumps in parallel.
chapters.trap: In series flow is the same through both pumps and heads add; in parallel head is the same across both pumps and flows add. Do not add both.
chapters.prereq: 7.3 heads and efficiencies; Unit 4 pipes in series and parallel for the same reasoning.
chapters.leave: Full characteristic curves to 7.6; NPSH to 7.5; pipe friction to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Cavitation happens when local pressure falls to vapour pressure; NPSH is the margin that keeps the pump from cavitating.
chapters.depth: Define NPSH available: NPSH_A = p_atm/(ρg) − p_v/(ρg) − H_s − h_fs for suction lift H_s positive. Define p_atm, p_v, ρ, g, h_fs. NPSH required comes from the maker. Use absolute pressures. Explain cavitation: bubbles form at the eye, collapse, cause noise, vibration, pitting and head drop. Condition for safe running: NPSH_A ≥ NPSH_R. Show effect of suction lift, water temperature and speed. Mention Thoma cavitation factor σ in one line if needed. No derivation of NPSH_R.

figure.aria: Suction lift and pipe losses reduce eye pressure; NPSH available is compared with NPSH required to decide whether cavitation is avoided.

chapters.example: A pump draws water at 30°C from a sump whose surface is 4 m below the pump centreline. The suction pipe friction loss is 1.2 m. Atmospheric pressure is 101 kPa and vapour pressure at 30°C is 4.2 kPa. Find NPSH available. Density of water is 996 kg/m³.
chapters.trap: Use absolute pressure and subtract suction lift and suction friction; a negative NPSH available is impossible and means cavitation.
chapters.prereq: 7.3 heads; Unit 1 pressure; Unit 4 pipe friction losses.
chapters.leave: Performance curves and NPSH required curve to 7.6; pipe friction details to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A pump's head, efficiency and power change with flow, and the curves show the safe duty point.
chapters.depth: Cover main characteristic: head vs Q (falling), efficiency vs Q (peak), power vs Q (rising for centrifugal), NPSH_R vs Q. Define system curve and duty point where pump head equals system head. Define rated point, shut-off head and run-out. Add pump specific speed N_s = N√Q/H^(3/4), with N in rpm, Q in m³/s and H in m; state that the number is dimensional and used to select radial, mixed or axial type. Cross-ref Unit 6 for turbine specific speed. Give affinity laws for the same pump at different speed: Q ∝ N, H ∝ N², P ∝ N³. Contrast briefly with a reciprocating pump, whose flow is almost constant and head varies.

figure.aria: The falling pump-head curve meets the rising system-head curve at the duty point near 35 L/s and 24 m.

chapters.example: A pump test at 1450 rpm gives head 40 m at 0 L/s, 38 m at 10 L/s, 34 m at 20 L/s, 28 m at 30 L/s and 20 m at 40 L/s. The system head is 12 m at 0 L/s, 13 m at 10 L/s, 16 m at 20 L/s, 21 m at 30 L/s and 28 m at 40 L/s. Plot both curves and estimate the duty flow and head.
chapters.trap: The duty point is where pump head equals system head, not the peak efficiency point unless the system curve also passes there.
chapters.prereq: 7.3 heads and efficiencies; 7.4 series and parallel; 7.5 NPSH; Unit 6 turbine specific speed for analogy.
chapters.leave: Cavitation to 7.5; slip to 7.7; air vessels to 7.8.

chapters.idea: A reciprocating pump traps a fixed volume and pushes it by a piston, so its ideal flow depends only on geometry and speed; slip is the difference from ideal.
chapters.depth: Cover single-acting and double-acting, piston or plunger, crank, connecting rod, suction and delivery valves. Theoretical flow Q_th = A L N/60 for single-acting; for double-acting with rod area a_r, Q_th = (2A − a_r)L N/60. Define A, L, N, a_r. Define slip = Q_th − Q_act, coefficient of discharge C_d = Q_act/Q_th, positive and negative slip. Draw ideal and actual indicator diagrams: suction and delivery strokes, effect of acceleration and friction, valve opening and separation. Include work done and power. No air-vessel derivation, which is 7.8.

figure.aria: Crank and piston motion creates suction and delivery strokes; theoretical flow comes from geometry, actual flow is measured, and slip is their difference.

chapters.example: A single-acting reciprocating pump has a cylinder diameter of 180 mm, stroke 300 mm and runs at 60 rpm. Its actual discharge is 6.5 L/s. Find the theoretical discharge, coefficient of discharge and percentage slip.
chapters.trap: Use N in rpm with the /60 in the formula; slip is theoretical minus actual, positive when actual is less.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 crank motion; Unit 1 pressure for indicator diagram.
chapters.leave: Air vessels and work saved to 7.8; pipe friction to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: An air vessel stores water during the fast part of the stroke and returns it during the slow part, smoothing flow and saving friction work.
chapters.depth: Cover location on suction and delivery pipes and the trapped air cushion. Explain why reciprocating flow is pulsating: velocity varies as sin θ for a single-acting pump. A large air vessel makes delivery flow nearly constant at the mean value. For work saved against delivery friction, use the single-acting results: without air vessel W_f = (2/3)ρgALh_f,max; with a large air vessel W_f = ρgALh_f,max/π²; saved ≈ 0.565ρgALh_f,max, about 84.8% of W_f. Define h_f,max as friction head at peak delivery velocity. Do not derive double-acting cases unless the syllabus asks.

figure.aria: A branch air vessel on the delivery pipe stores water on the fast stroke and returns it on the slow stroke, giving steadier delivery.

chapters.example: A single-acting reciprocating pump has cylinder area 0.03 m², stroke 0.30 m and speed 60 rpm. The maximum friction head in the delivery pipe is 6 m. Find the work done against friction per stroke without an air vessel and with a large air vessel, and the percentage saved. Take ρ = 1000 kg/m³.
chapters.trap: Do not use mean friction head in the without-air-vessel work; friction head varies as sin²θ, so the standard factor is 2/3.
chapters.prereq: 7.7 reciprocating pump and indicator diagram; Unit 4 pipe friction.
chapters.leave: Slip and indicator diagram to 7.7; pipe friction details to Unit 4.
